lesson.title: Why a Whisper Matters More in a Quiet Room
lesson.summary: Weber's Law states that the just noticeable difference between two stimuli is a constant proportion of the original stimulus, explaining why the same absolute change can feel huge in one context and unnoticeable in another.
lesson.body:
Once psychologists could reliably measure the Difference Threshold, or just noticeable difference, for various stimuli, a pattern emerged that seemed almost too tidy to be a coincidence. The amount a stimulus needs to change before the change is detectable is not a fixed quantity. Instead, it is a constant proportion, or percentage, of the original stimulus's intensity. This relationship is known as Weber's Law, and it explains why the same absolute change in a stimulus can be easy to notice in one situation and completely unnoticeable in another, depending on how intense the starting stimulus already is.

A concrete illustration makes this intuitive. Imagine a room lit by a single candle. Adding one more candle roughly doubles the light, and the increase is obvious. Now imagine a room already blazing with a hundred candles. Adding one more candle produces the same absolute increase in light, one extra candle's worth, but the change is now imperceptible, because it represents a tiny fraction of the room's total illumination rather than a doubling of it. Weber's Law captures this precisely: what matters for detectability is not the raw amount added, but the ratio between the amount added and the amount already present.

This proportional relationship holds, at least approximately, across many types of stimuli, though the exact proportion, sometimes called the Weber fraction, differs from sense to sense and from one type of stimulus to another. Detecting a change in weight might require a smaller percentage increase than detecting a change in loudness, for instance, but within a given sensory dimension, the proportional rule tends to hold reasonably well across a wide middle range of intensities, even though it can break down at very low or very high extremes.

Weber's Law has genuine practical consequences that extend well beyond the psychology laboratory. It is part of why a modest pay raise feels significant to someone earning very little but negligible to someone already earning a great deal, and why a small price increase on an inexpensive item draws more complaints than the same dollar increase on an expensive one. It also explains a common perceptual experience: turning up the volume on a nearly silent stereo produces a much more noticeable jump in loudness than the same volume increase applied to already loud music.

The deeper significance of Weber's Law is what it reveals about how the nervous system encodes intensity in the first place. Sensory systems appear to represent stimulus intensity in a relative, comparative way rather than as a simple linear readout of physical energy, which fits neatly with the broader theme introduced by the difference threshold, that sensation is fundamentally built to register change and contrast rather than to serve as a precise, literal measuring instrument.
